kurals.tamil:
வாய்மை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
தீமை இலாத சொலல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Vaaymai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Theemai ilaadha solal.
kurals.meaning: If you ask what truthfulness really is, it is speaking words that bring no harm of any kind to anyone.
kurals.elementary: Being truthful isn’t only about not telling lies. Imagine your words are like gifts you hand to people — a truthful gift is one that never hurts anybody. So truth means saying things that are real AND that don’t cause harm.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately surprising definition: vaaymai is not defined by correspondence to fact (the usual Western criterion) but by its effect — speech ‘without even the least evil’ (yaadhondrum theemai ilaadha). The standard commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah) all read theemai as harm to others, so truth becomes an ethical rather than merely epistemic category. This places the Kural within the broader Indian tradition that fuses satya with ahimsa, and it sets up the controversial next couplet (292) on beneficial untruth. The verse’s rhetorical form — a question answered in a definition (enappaduvadhu yaadhenin, ‘if one asks what is called…’) — marks it as the chapter’s thesis statement.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Words that do not cause distress, are truthful, inoffensive, and beneficial, as well as regular recitation of the Vedic scriptures—these are declared as austerity of speech.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna defines the discipline of speech as words that are true AND do not upset or harm the listener. The commentary on this verse also cites Manu 4.138: speak the truth, speak what is pleasing, do not speak an unpleasant truth.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Gita builds harmlessness into the very definition of right, truthful speech.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close: truthfulness joined to ‘not causing distress’ (anudvega-karam). The Gita lists truth and harmlessness as twin requirements, while the Kural folds harmlessness into the definition of truth itself.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Let no corrupt communication proceed out of your mouth, but that which is good to the use of edifying, that it may minister grace unto the hearers.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers that every word should build people up and do them good, never tear them down.
christianity.tie_back: Both texts judge speech by its effect on the hearer: good speech ‘ministers grace,’ never harm.
christianity._accuracy_note: Shares the harm-free standard for speech, though Paul is talking about speech generally, not defining truthfulness. Ephesians 4:15 (‘speaking the truth in love’) is the closer thematic pairing.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, fear Allāh and speak words of appropriate justice.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an asks believers to speak ‘qawlan sadīdan’ — speech that is straight, true, and right, the next verse promising that God will set their deeds right in return.
islam.tie_back: ‘Appropriate, just’ speech unites truth with rightness toward others, echoing the Kural’s harmless truth.
islam._accuracy_note: Qawl sadid includes both accuracy and fairness; it does not explicitly define truth as harmlessness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Speak ye every man the truth to his neighbour; execute the judgment of truth and peace in your gates.”
judaism.explanation: The prophet Zechariah joins truth and peace as a pair: speaking truth is meant to build a peaceful community.
judaism.tie_back: Truth in Zechariah is always paired with peace, just as the Kural pairs it with harmlessness.
judaism._accuracy_note: Truth and peace are coupled but not merged into one definition as in the Kural.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Speak only the speech that neither torments self nor does harm to others. That speech is truly well spoken.”
buddhism.explanation: In the Subhasita Sutta, Vangisa praises the Buddha’s teaching that good speech must hurt neither the speaker nor anyone else; the same verses call truth ‘deathless speech.’
buddhism.tie_back: Almost the Kural’s definition: right speech is speech free of harm, grounded in truth.
buddhism.source: Subhasita Sutta, Sutta Nipata 3.3 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one: harmlessness to others as the test of well-spoken, truthful speech.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “And Sea begat Nereus, the eldest of his children, who is true and lies not: and men call him the Old Man because he is trusty and gentle and does not forget the laws of righteousness, but thinks just and kindly thoughts.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod’s Nereus, the ‘Old Man of the Sea,’ is the Greek god famed for never lying — and Hesiod pairs his truthfulness with gentleness and kindly thoughts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Nereus embodies truth that is also gentle and kind — truth without harm.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: A portrait of truthful, gentle character rather than a definition of truth; the pairing of truth with kindness is the real link.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Immanuel Kant, in his 1797 essay ‘On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy,’ argued that truthfulness in all statements is an unconditional duty of reason — one may not lie even to a murderer asking where a friend is hiding.
philosophy.explanation: Kant defines truthfulness purely as not asserting falsehood, whatever the consequences to others.
philosophy.tie_back: An instructive contrast: Kant defines truth by the statement, Valluvar by its effect on others — and would likely judge Kant’s truthful answer to the murderer as not vaaymai at all.
philosophy.source: Kant, On a Supposed Right to Lie (1797)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Deliberate contrast, not a parallel: Kant’s absolutism is the opposite pole from the Kural’s harm-based definition.

kurals.tamil:
பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த புரைதீர்ந்த
நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்.
kurals.transliteration:
Poymaiyum vaaymai yidaththa puraitheerndha
Nanmai payakkum enin.
kurals.meaning: Even a falsehood can take the place of truth, if it produces good that is wholly free of fault.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a friend is scared before a big test and asks if they look nervous. Saying “You look calm and ready!” — to help them, not to trick them for your own gain — is the kind of “kind untruth” this kural talks about. But it only counts if it does real good and hurts no one.
kurals.university: This is one of the most debated couplets in the Kural. Having defined truth by harmlessness in 291, Valluvar draws the logical consequence: a statement that is factually false but yields ‘faultless good’ (puraitheerndha nanmai) occupies ‘the place of truth’ (vaaymai idaththa). The qualifier purai theerndha — ‘with the defect removed’ — is strict: the good must be free of any taint, not merely useful to the speaker. Commentators diverge on scope: Varadarasan says such words ‘obtain the place’ of truth; Pappaiah reads it as permission to speak falsely where truth would otherwise be required. The verse places the Kural in a consequentialist line of Indian ethics (compare Krishna’s teaching in the Mahabharata) rather than the absolutism of Kant or of Buddhist precept.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Truth may be unutterable, and even falsehood may be utterable where falsehood would become truth and truth would become falsehood.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna tells Arjuna the story of the ascetic Kausika, who had vowed always to speak the truth. When robbers asked him which way their fleeing victims had gone, he told them truthfully; the victims were killed, and Kausika fell into hell for the harm his ‘truth’ caused.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s logic: a harmful ‘truth’ ceases to be truth, and a harmless untruth can take truth’s place.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Karna Parva, Section 69 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact parallel, even in phrasing: ‘falsehood would become truth.’ Krishna’s list of permitted lies is narrower and more situational than the Kural’s general principle.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Likewise also was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way?”
christianity.explanation: Rahab hid Israel’s spies and misled the king’s men to save their lives (Joshua 2); the New Testament praises her as justified by her deed.
christianity.tie_back: A deception that saved innocent lives is honoured — close to the Kural’s ‘faultless good.’
christianity._accuracy_note: Christian interpreters differ: many (e.g., Augustine) praise Rahab’s faith and kindness but not the lie itself. The verse does not explicitly endorse falsehood.

islam.quote_or_event: “He who makes peace between the people by inventing good information or saying good things, is not a liar.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that someone who carries good (even embellished) words between quarrelling people to reconcile them is not counted a liar.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, Islam allows a narrowly bounded untruth when its fruit is pure good — here, peace.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match; the Islamic exemption is limited to specific cases (reconciliation, and in other reports war and spouses), while the Kural states a general principle.

judaism.quote_or_event: “It is permitted for a person to depart from the truth in a matter that will bring peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud cites Joseph’s brothers, and even God’s softened report of Sarah’s words to Abraham, as examples of altering the truth to preserve peace. Rabbi Natan calls it a mitzvah.
judaism.tie_back: Jewish law, like the Kural, lets a peace-making untruth stand in truth’s place.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Yevamot 65b (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz tr.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; the rabbinic exemption is tied specifically to peace (shalom), a subset of the Kural’s ‘faultless good.’

buddhism.quote_or_event: “In the case of words that the Tathagata knows to be unfactual, untrue, unbeneficial, but endearing & agreeable to others, he does not say them.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha lists which words he will speak: only what is true and beneficial, with a sense of the proper time. As the translator notes, the possibility of saying something untrue but beneficial is not even considered.
buddhism.tie_back: An honest contrast: early Buddhism shares the Kural’s concern for benefit, but will never allow falsehood to take truth’s place.
buddhism.source: Abhaya Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 58 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial contrast: shared benefit test, opposite conclusion on beneficial untruths (later Mahayana upaya teaching comes closer to the Kural).

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “We know how to speak many false things as though they were true; but we know, when we will, to utter true things.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The Muses tell Hesiod that they can speak convincing falsehoods as well as truth — the divine source of poetry itself deals in both.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Greek myth, like the Kural, recognises that falsehood can wear truth’s clothing — though the Muses do not limit it to ‘faultless good.’
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak match: acknowledges truth-like falsehood but adds no moral test of benefit.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic (389b), Socrates says falsehood is useless to the gods but may be useful to humans ‘as a medicine,’ and that only the rulers may use it, for the good of the city.
philosophy.explanation: Plato accepts a ‘medicinal lie’ for the common good, while condemning the ‘true lie’ of self-deception in the soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Both Plato and Valluvar allow falsehood when it heals rather than harms — though Plato restricts it to rulers.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good structural parallel (beneficial falsehood), but Plato’s version is political and elite-restricted, while the Kural’s is personal and universal.

kurals.tamil:
தன்நெஞ் சறிவது பொய்யற்க பொய்த்தபின்
தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Than nenju arivadhu poyyarka poyththapin
Than nenjae thannaich chudum.
kurals.meaning: Do not lie about what your own heart knows to be true; once you have lied, your own heart will burn you.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever told a fib and then felt a hot, uncomfortable feeling inside, even if no one found out? That feeling is your own heart “burning” you. This kural says: don’t lie against what you know is true, because your conscience will punish you.
kurals.university: The couplet moves truthfulness from the social sphere into the interior. ‘Than nenju arivadhu’ — what one’s own heart knows — specifies a deliberate lie, one told against one’s own knowledge. The punishment is not external: ‘than nenjae thannaich chudum,’ the self’s own heart scorches the self. The repetition of than (self) three times across two lines enacts the reflexive structure of conscience. Kalaignar explicitly glosses nenju as manachaatchi, ‘conscience,’ and Pappaiah adds that the burning intensifies when the world discovers the lie — combining inner guilt with outer shame.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The Soul itself is the witness of the Soul, and the Soul is the refuge of the Soul; despise not thy own Soul, the supreme witness of men.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu warns witnesses in court not to lie, because their own inner self is the highest witness; the next verse says the wicked think no one sees them, but the gods and ‘the male within their own breasts’ see them.
hinduism.tie_back: Both texts make the inner self the witness and judge of every lie.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close: the inner witness is the same; Manu’s context is courtroom testimony, while the Kural’s is universal.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if our heart condemn us, God is greater than our heart, and knoweth all things. Beloved, if our heart condemn us not, then have we confidence toward God.”
christianity.explanation: John describes the heart as an inner court that condemns or acquits us, with God knowing even more than our heart.
christianity.tie_back: The self-accusing heart is the Kural’s burning heart.
christianity._accuracy_note: Same image of a heart that condemns; John’s context is love and obedience in general, not lying specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “Leave what makes you in doubt for what does not make you in doubt. The truth brings tranquility while falsehood sows doubt.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that truth settles the heart while lying leaves it restless and troubled.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘burning heart’ after a lie is Islam’s ‘doubt’ that falsehood sows within.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong psychological parallel: lying disturbs the inner self, truth calms it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “LORD, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? who shall dwell in thy holy hill? He that walketh uprightly, and worketh righteousness, and speaketh the truth in his heart.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist says the one fit to stand before God speaks truth ‘in his heart’ — inner words agreeing with outer ones.
judaism.tie_back: Both demand that speech never betray what the heart knows.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the heart-truth link; the Psalm stresses reward, the Kural the inner punishment.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When anyone feels no shame in telling a deliberate lie, there is no evil, I tell you, he will not do.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches his young son Rahula that shamelessness about deliberate lies empties a person of spiritual worth, and tells him to reflect on every action like looking in a mirror.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s burning heart is exactly the healthy shame the Buddha wants Rahula to keep.
buddhism.source: Ambalatthika-rahulovada Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 61 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close: both focus on deliberate lies and inner conscience; the Buddha frames it as shame that protects, the Kural as pain that punishes.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “For hateful in my eyes, even as the gates of Hades, is that man that hideth one thing in his mind and sayeth another.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Achilles tells Odysseus he despises anyone whose words differ from what is in his mind.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Achilles condemns the same split the Kural forbids: saying what the heart knows is false.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Same target (speech against one’s mind), but Achilles condemns the liar from outside rather than describing the liar’s inner torment.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In the Republic (382a-c), Socrates distinguishes the ‘true lie’ — falsehood lodged in the soul about the most important things — which gods and men hate above all, from the mere lie in words.
philosophy.explanation: For Plato, the worst harm of falsehood is to the liar’s own soul.
philosophy.tie_back: Both thinkers locate the deepest damage of lying inside the liar.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Related but different: Plato’s ‘true lie’ is self-deception or ignorance, while the Kural’s liar knows the truth and is burned by that knowledge.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யா தொழுகின் உலகத்தார்
உள்ளத்து ளெல்லாம் உளன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullaththaal poyyaadhu ozhukin ulagaththaar
Ullaththul ellaam ulan.
kurals.meaning: One who lives without falsehood even in his heart will dwell in the hearts of all the people of the world.
kurals.elementary: Think of someone you completely trust — a grandparent or a teacher who never tricks you. You carry them in your heart, don’t you? This kural says that if you are honest even inside your own thoughts, everyone will keep you in their hearts too.
kurals.university: The couplet is built on an elegant chiasmus of ullam (heart/mind): one who does not lie ‘with the heart’ (ullaththaal) comes to live ‘in the hearts’ (ullaththul) of all. Truthfulness here extends past speech to conduct (ozhukin, ‘if one conducts oneself’) and even to thought — Kalaignar reads it as not even thinking falsehood. The reward is not wealth or heaven but a permanent place in human regard, which links this chapter to the preceding chapter on fame (புகழ், ch. 24). Pappaiah narrows ‘ulagaththaar’ to the noble (uyarndhavar), following the classical reading of ulagam as ‘the worthy.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: King Harishchandra, who kept his word at the cost of his kingdom, his family and his freedom, is remembered across India as ‘Satya Harishchandra’ — the very name a byword for truthfulness. Gandhi wrote that the play about him shaped his lifelong devotion to truth.
hinduism.explanation: The Puranic king who refused to break his word even in utter ruin became a permanent hero in the popular imagination.
hinduism.tie_back: Harishchandra is the Kural’s promise fulfilled: truthfulness made him dwell in the hearts of all people.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Illustrative story rather than a statement of principle; the match lies in its enduring place in popular memory.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus saw Nathanael coming to him, and saith of him, Behold an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile!”
christianity.explanation: Jesus singles out Nathanael for praise because there is no deceit in him at all.
christianity.tie_back: A heart without guile wins the highest regard — the Kural’s reward.
christianity._accuracy_note: Praise for inner guilelessness, but no claim about dwelling in the hearts of all people.

islam.quote_or_event: “And grant me a mention [i.e., reputation] of honor among later generations.”
islam.explanation: Abraham prays for a good name among later generations; the Arabic is ‘lisāna ṣidqin,’ literally ‘a tongue of truth.’
islam.tie_back: The truthful prophet asks for exactly the Kural’s reward: to live on in the regard of all people.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match through the root ṣ-d-q (truth): a lasting ‘truthful’ reputation. The verse is a prayer, not a general law.

judaism.quote_or_event: “The lip of truth shall be established for ever: but a lying tongue is but for a moment.”
judaism.explanation: Proverbs says truthful speech lasts forever, while lies pass away quickly.
judaism.tie_back: Truth gives a lasting place in the world; lies vanish — the same contrast as the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Shares the idea of truth’s permanence but speaks of the words enduring, not the person living in others’ hearts.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “People hold dear him who embodies virtue and insight, who is principled, has realized the truth, and who himself does what he ought to be doing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada says the one people cherish is virtuous and truthful (the Pali saccavādin also means ‘truth-speaker’).
buddhism.tie_back: Being held dear by all people is the Kural’s ‘dwelling in their hearts.’
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close in outcome (being loved by people); Buddharakkhita renders the truth element as ‘realized the truth’ rather than ‘speaks truth.’

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Whoever deliberately lies in his witness and forswears himself… that man’s generation is left obscure thereafter. But the generation of the man who swears truly is better thenceforward.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Hesiod teaches his brother that the liar’s family sinks into obscurity, while the truthful man’s line prospers and is remembered.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Truthfulness earns a lasting good name among people; lies bring oblivion.
greek_mythology.source: Hesiod, Works and Days 280-285 (tr. H. G. Evelyn-White)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Parallel reward structure (lasting standing), but Hesiod focuses on oaths and family fortune rather than inner honesty.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle describes the truthful man as one who is true in word and in life even where nothing is at stake, simply because his character is such — and who will therefore be all the more truthful where much is at stake.
philosophy.explanation: For Aristotle, truthfulness is a settled state of character, not a calculation.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘not lying with the heart’ is Aristotle’s truthfulness rooted in character.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (paraphrase of W. D. Ross tr.)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the inner-character aspect; Aristotle does not promise the social reward the Kural names.

kurals.tamil:
மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின் தவத்தொடு
தானஞ்செய் வாரின் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaththodu vaaymai mozhiyin thavaththodu
Thaanam seyvaarin thalai.
kurals.meaning: One who speaks truth in harmony with his heart stands above those who practise both austerity and charity.
kurals.elementary: Some people do hard things to look holy, like fasting, and some give lots of gifts. This kural says that someone who simply speaks the truth from the heart, every day, is even greater than people who do both of those big things.
kurals.university: Here Valluvar ranks truthfulness above the two most prestigious religious practices of his world: thavam (tapas, ascetic austerity, the subject of chapter 27) and dhaanam (charity/gift-giving). The qualifier manaththodu — ‘together with the mind’ — is decisive: only truth that agrees with inner conviction counts, not lip-truth (Kalaignar: ‘udhattalavil indri ulamaara,’ ‘not just from the lips but from the heart’). The couplet belongs to a broad pan-Indian and wider religious critique of ritualism, in which inner integrity outweighs outer observance. Its hierarchy — truth above tapas — is stated almost verbatim in the Mahabharata’s image of truth outweighing a hundred horse-sacrifices.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “A hundred horse-sacrifices had once been weighed against Truth, and Truth was found heavier than a hundred horse-sacrifices.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala, rejected by King Dushmanta, reminds him that truth outweighs even the greatest Vedic rituals — equal, she says, to studying all the Vedas and bathing at every holy place.
hinduism.tie_back: Exactly the Kural’s ranking: truthfulness weighs more than the grandest religious works.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 74 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-exact: truth weighed above sacrifice; the Kural names austerity and charity instead of the horse-sacrifice.

christianity.quote_or_event: “God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that true worship is not about the right mountain or temple, but about spirit and truth.
christianity.tie_back: Inner truth, not outward religious performance, is what counts most.
christianity._accuracy_note: Truth over external ritual; ‘truth’ in John is broader (sincerity and divine reality), not truthful speech specifically.

islam.quote_or_event: “Righteousness is not that you turn your faces toward the east or the west, but [true] righteousness is [in] one who believes in Allāh… Those are the ones who have been true, and it is those who are the righteous.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an says real righteousness is not the direction you face in prayer, but faith, generosity, keeping promises and patience — and it calls such people ‘the ones who have been true.’
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, the verse places inner truthfulness above outward ritual form.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on truth over ritual form; the Qur’an includes charity within righteousness rather than ranking truth above it.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.”
judaism.explanation: In his psalm of repentance David says God wants truth deep inside a person; a few verses later he adds that God does not delight in burnt offerings but in a broken and contrite heart (51:16-17).
judaism.tie_back: Inner truth over sacrifice — the Kural’s ‘truth with the heart’ above austerity and gifts.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong: truth ‘in the inward parts’ matches ‘manaththodu,’ and the psalm explicitly ranks it above sacrifice.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not by matted hair, nor by lineage, nor by birth does one become a holy man. But he in whom truth and righteousness exist — he is pure, he is a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha rejects the outward marks of ascetics; the next verse mocks the man in antelope skins who ‘only outwardly’ cleanses himself.
buddhism.tie_back: Truth, not ascetic show, makes a person holy — the Kural’s point about austerity.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Close: truth ranked over ascetic appearance; charity is not mentioned.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: At Mecone, Prometheus tricked Zeus into choosing bones wrapped in fat rather than meat, and Hesiod explains this deception as the origin of how humans offer sacrifice — the ritual itself is born from a lie.
greek_mythology.explanation: In Greek myth the central religious ritual, animal sacrifice, is rooted in a trick played on the gods.
greek_mythology.tie_back: A sideways contrast: Greek myth shows ritual without truth at its origin, while the Kural insists truth outranks ritual.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Weak, contrastive match: no Greek myth directly ranks truthfulness above sacrifice; this story shows ritual detached from truth.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He who lies is guilty of impiety to the same divinity; for the universal nature is the nature of things that are.”
philosophy.explanation: Marcus Aurelius argues that because Nature itself is truth, lying is a sin against the divine — honesty is the true piety.
philosophy.tie_back: For the Stoic, as for Valluvar, truthfulness is itself the highest religious act.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Truthfulness equated with piety; Marcus does not explicitly rank it above austerity or charity.

kurals.tamil:
பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை எய்யாமை
எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Poyyaamai anna pugazhillai eyyaamai
Ellaa aramum tharum.
kurals.meaning: There is no fame like that of never lying; without any strain, it brings every other virtue along with it.
kurals.elementary: Being known as someone who never lies is the best reputation you can have. And it’s like a magnet — once you are truthful, other good habits, like fairness and kindness, come to you easily, without you even trying hard.
kurals.university: The couplet makes two claims: truthfulness is the supreme source of pugazh (fame, cf. ch. 24), and it ‘yields every dharma’ (ellaa aramum tharum). The pivot word eyyaamai is read in two ways: Parimelazhagar-line commentators take it as ‘without suffering/strain’ — truthfulness produces all virtue effortlessly, unlike painful austerity; Varadarasan and Pappaiah read it as ‘without one’s knowing it,’ i.e., the virtues accrue unnoticed. Either way the claim is that veracity is a generative, master virtue from which the others follow — a thesis close to the Islamic hadith that truthfulness leads to righteousness.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The true prevails, not the untrue; by the true the path is laid out, the way of the gods.”
hinduism.explanation: The Mundaka Upanishad — source of India’s national motto ‘Satyameva Jayate’ — says truth wins, and that truth itself lays down the road to the divine.
hinduism.tie_back: Truth that triumphs and opens the path to every good echoes the Kural’s truth that brings unmatched fame and all virtues.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Truth’s supremacy and its road to the highest good match well; the idea of ‘fame’ is not present.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore putting away lying, speak every man truth with his neighbour: for we are members one of another.”
christianity.explanation: Paul makes truth-telling the first step of the new life, because believers belong to one another like parts of one body.
christianity.tie_back: Truthfulness as the foundation from which the rest of the moral life grows.
christianity._accuracy_note: Truth is foundational here, but the passage does not speak of fame or of truth generating all virtues.

islam.quote_or_event: “…the truthful men and truthful women… for them Allāh has prepared forgiveness and a great reward.”
islam.explanation: Among the qualities God praises in believing men and women, truthfulness appears alongside patience, charity and fasting, all promised a great reward.
islam.tie_back: Truthfulness earns the highest honour — divine praise and reward.
islam._accuracy_note: Truthfulness is honoured, but listed alongside other virtues rather than as their source. (Bukhari 6094, under Kural 297, captures the generative claim.)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabban Shimon ben Gamaliel used to say: on three things does the world stand: On justice, on truth and on peace.”
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah names truth as one of the three pillars that hold up the whole world.
judaism.tie_back: Truth as a foundation supporting everything else — the Kural’s ‘brings all virtues.’
judaism._accuracy_note: Truth is foundational, but shares the role with justice and peace; no reference to personal fame.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “He who utters gentle, instructive and truthful words, who imprecates none — him do I call a holy man.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha gives truthful, gentle speech as one mark of the true brahmin, the person worthy of the highest honour.
buddhism.tie_back: Truthful speech earns the highest title of respect.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Truthfulness confers honour; it is one mark among many rather than the source of all virtue.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Muse, you and the daughter of Zeus, unforgetting Truth: with the hand that puts things right, keep from me the blame for lying, for wronging my friend.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar calls on Aletheia (Truth), daughter of Zeus, to protect his reputation from the blame of a broken promise.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In Greek thought Truth is a goddess who guards a person’s good name — the Kural’s link between truth and fame.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Truth tied to reputation; the ‘all virtues’ claim is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “And falsehood is in itself mean and culpable, and truth noble and worthy of praise.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle states that truthfulness is by its very nature noble and deserves praise.
philosophy.tie_back: Truth is ‘worthy of praise’ in itself — the Kural’s ‘no fame like truthfulness.’
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics 4.7 (tr. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on praise; Aristotle does not claim truthfulness generates the other virtues.

kurals.tamil:
பொய்யாமை பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற
செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று.
kurals.transliteration:
Poyyaamai poyyaamai aatrin aram pira
Seyyaamai seyyaamai nandru.
kurals.meaning: If one practises truthfulness without ever failing in it, it is well even if one does no other virtuous deed.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a report card where one subject counts so much that getting it right is enough to pass everything. For Valluvar, truthfulness is that subject: if you never fail at being honest, you’re doing well even if you haven’t done any other good deeds yet.
kurals.university: A celebrated example of Valluvar’s wordplay: poyyaamai poyyaamai (literally ‘non-lying, not failing’) and seyyaamai seyyaamai (‘not doing, not doing’). The first pair means practising non-falsehood unfailingly; the second is read by most commentators (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) as ‘not doing [other virtues] is itself not a lack’ — truth alone suffices. Varadarasan offers a softer reading (‘practising other virtues also becomes good’), and Kalaignar reads it as truthfulness surpassing the merit of mere abstentions. The dominant reading makes veracity a sufficient condition of the good life, the strongest claim in the chapter after 300.

hinduism.explanation: Patanjali teaches that when a person is firmly established in truthfulness, actions and their fruits come to rest on him — commentators say his words and deeds become effective by truth alone.
hinduism.tie_back: Truthfulness alone, fully established, makes all action bear fruit — like the Kural’s claim that truth alone suffices.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Satya as a self-sufficient power; the sutra describes a yogic attainment, not a claim that other virtues are unnecessary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus promises that living in the truth brings freedom from sin and bondage.
christianity.tie_back: Truth alone has the power to liberate — close to the Kural’s truth that is enough by itself.
christianity._accuracy_note: ‘Truth’ in John means divine revelation in Christ rather than truthful speech; the parallel is in truth’s sufficiency.

islam.quote_or_event: “Truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. And a man keeps on telling the truth until he becomes a truthful person.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet taught that steady truthfulness leads step by step to all righteousness and finally to Paradise, while lying leads to wickedness and the Fire.
islam.tie_back: Keep truthfulness unfailingly, and the rest of goodness follows — the Kural’s point exactly.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close: persistence in truth (‘keeps on telling the truth’) mirrors poyyaamai poyyaamai, and truth leads to all righteousness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Keep thee far from a false matter; and the innocent and righteous slay thou not: for I will not justify the wicked.”
judaism.explanation: The Torah does not merely forbid falsehood — it commands keeping far away from it, an unusually strong phrasing rabbinic tradition often notes.
judaism.tie_back: Unfailing distance from falsehood as a core command echoes the Kural’s unfailing non-lying.
judaism._accuracy_note: Stresses the seriousness of avoiding falsehood; says nothing about truth being sufficient on its own.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “For a liar who has violated the one law (of truthfulness) who holds in scorn the hereafter, there is no evil that he cannot do.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada calls truthfulness ‘the one law’: break it, and every other evil becomes possible.
buddhism.tie_back: The mirror image of the Kural: keep this one virtue and all is well; break it and all is lost.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong: truth as the single keystone virtue, stated negatively.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Hesiod says that when a god swears falsely by the waters of Styx he lies breathless for a year, is barred from nectar and ambrosia, and is cut off from the gods’ councils and feasts for nine more years.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even immortals keep one law above all: their sworn word by the Styx must never be false.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Among the gods, truthfulness to one’s oath is the one indispensable law, as truthfulness is for Valluvar.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Truthfulness in oaths as supreme; narrower (oaths only) and punitive rather than a claim of sufficiency.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “From me you shall hear the whole truth.”
philosophy.explanation: At his trial Socrates refuses flattery and rhetoric, offering only the truth — and dies rather than abandon it.
philosophy.tie_back: Socrates staked his whole life on one commitment, truth, and considered it enough.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Illustrates truth held as the single guiding commitment; not a doctrine that other virtues are optional.

kurals.tamil:
புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும் அகந்தூய்மை
வாய்மையால் காணப் படும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Purandhooymai neeraan amaiyum agandhooymai
Vaaymaiyaal kaanap padum.
kurals.meaning: Outer purity comes from water; inner purity is seen through truthfulness.
kurals.elementary: When you get muddy, you take a bath and you’re clean on the outside. But how do you get clean on the inside? This kural says water can’t reach there — only telling the truth can wash your mind and heart.
kurals.university: The couplet sets up a clean binary: puram / agam (outer / inner), a pairing that also names the two great genres of classical Tamil poetry. Outer purity ‘is achieved’ (amaiyum) by water; inner purity ‘is seen / made manifest’ (kaanappadum) by truthfulness — truth both produces and reveals a clean mind. This is a pointed comment on ritual bathing (neeraadal) in holy waters. Textual note: several popular web editions print the first word as ‘புறள்தூய்மை’; the grammatically regular form ‘புறந்தூய்மை’ (puram + thooymai), used here, is attested in other editions and fits the parallel with அகந்தூய்மை.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “The body is cleansed by water, the internal organ is purified by truthfulness, the individual soul by sacred learning and austerities, the intellect by (true) knowledge.”
hinduism.explanation: Manu lists what purifies each part of a person: water for the body, truthfulness for the mind.
hinduism.tie_back: Practically word for word the Kural’s claim: water cleans the outside, truth cleans the inside.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical statement; Manu goes on to add further purifiers for soul and intellect.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou blind Pharisee, cleanse first that which is within the cup and platter, that the outside of them may be clean also.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus rebukes religious leaders for washing the outside of cups while their hearts are full of greed and deceit.
christianity.tie_back: Inner cleansing matters more than outer washing — the Kural’s agam/puram contrast.
christianity._accuracy_note: Very close on inner vs. outer purity; the inner impurity named is greed and excess, with hypocrisy (a form of falsehood) the wider theme.

islam.quote_or_event: “But only one who comes to Allāh with a sound heart.”
islam.explanation: Abraham says that on Judgment Day neither wealth nor children will help — only a sound, pure heart.
islam.tie_back: Inner soundness of heart is what truly counts, beyond outward purity.
islam._accuracy_note: Inner purity is emphasised, but the verse contrasts it with wealth and offspring, not water or truth specifically. (Islam values both: wudu for the body, sincerity for the heart.)

judaism.quote_or_event: “Who shall ascend into the hill of the LORD? or who shall stand in his holy place? He that hath clean hands, and a pure heart; who hath not lifted up his soul unto vanity, nor sworn deceitfully.”
judaism.explanation: The psalm says entry to God’s presence requires clean hands AND a pure heart — and defines the pure heart as one that has not sworn deceitfully.
judaism.tie_back: Outer cleanness (hands) and inner purity (truthfulness) — exactly the Kural’s two purities.
judaism._accuracy_note: Excellent structural match; ‘clean hands’ refers to deeds rather than washing with water.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “It is here, O brahman, that you should bathe to make yourself a safe refuge for all beings. And if you speak no untruth, nor work any harm for breathing things… To Gaya gone, what would it do for you? Let any well your Gaya be!”
buddhism.explanation: When a brahmin asks whether the Buddha bathes in sacred rivers to wash away sin, the Buddha replies that true bathing is not lying and not harming — then any ordinary well is as holy as Gaya.
buddhism.tie_back: Truthfulness, not river water, is the real purifying bath — the Kural’s exact point.
buddhism.source: Vatthupama Sutta, Majjhima Nikaya 7 (tr. Nyanaponika Thera)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Near-exact: sacred-water bathing contrasted with inner purification by truthfulness and harmlessness.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Into an odorous temple, he who goes / Should pure and holy be; but to be wise / In what to sanctity pertains, is to be pure.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Porphyry quotes the inscription on the doors of the temple of Asclepius at Epidaurus: real purity is holiness of mind, not just a washed body and clean clothes.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Greek temple, like the Kural, ranks inner purity above outer cleansing.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong inner/outer purity match; the inscription names holy thought rather than truthfulness specifically.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Beloved Pan, and all ye other gods who haunt this place, give me beauty in the inward soul; and may the outward and inward man be at one.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates closes the Phaedrus praying that his inner soul be beautiful and that his outer self match it.
philosophy.tie_back: Inner beauty first, and outer and inner in harmony — the Kural’s concern for agam over puram.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Inner/outer harmony is central; truthfulness is implied (no gap between inner and outer) rather than named.

kurals.tamil:
எல்லா விளக்கும் விளக்கல்ல சான்றோர்க்குப்
பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Ellaa vilakkum vilakkalla saandrorkkup
Poyyaa vilakke vilakku.
kurals.meaning: Not every lamp is a true lamp; for the wise, the lamp of truthfulness alone is the real lamp.
kurals.elementary: A flashlight helps you see in a dark room. But what helps you see the right thing to do when you are confused inside? This kural says truthfulness is that special inner flashlight — and for wise people, it’s the only lamp that really matters.
kurals.university: The couplet repeats vilakku (lamp) four times, playing on its meanings: ordinary lamps dispel outer darkness, but ‘the lamp that does not lie’ (poyyaa vilakku) dispels inner darkness. Varadarasan’s gloss adds the parenthetical contrast explicitly: lamps that remove darkness outside versus the lamp of non-falsehood that removes darkness within. Saandror — the noble, the wise — is a key Kural term (cf. ch. 99, Saandraanmai), suggesting truthfulness is the defining light of the fully mature person. The truth-as-light metaphor is among the most widely shared images across religious traditions.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “From evil lead me to good, From darkness lead me to light, From death lead me to immortality.”
hinduism.explanation: This ancient prayer (‘asato mā sad gamaya, tamaso mā jyotir gamaya’) pairs moving from untruth (asat) to truth (sat) with moving from darkness to light.
hinduism.tie_back: Truth and light are one movement — the Kural’s lamp of truth.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Truth and light are closely linked; Madhavananda renders ‘asat/sat’ as evil/good (others translate unreal/real or falsehood/truth), and the Upanishad itself glosses the whole prayer as ‘make me immortal.’

christianity.quote_or_event: “If we say that we have fellowship with him, and walk in darkness, we lie, and do not the truth.”
christianity.explanation: John says that walking in darkness while claiming to be close to God is itself a lie; ‘God is light’ (1:5), and walking in the light means living in truth.
christianity.tie_back: Truth and light belong together, falsehood and darkness together — the Kural’s image.
christianity._accuracy_note: Clear light/truth vs. darkness/lie pairing; the Kural speaks of the wise man’s inner lamp rather than fellowship with God.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh is the Light of the heavens and the earth. The example of His light is like a niche within which is a lamp… Light upon light.”
islam.explanation: The famous Verse of Light describes God’s guidance as a perfect lamp lighting the heart of the believer.
islam.tie_back: A lamp of divine truth that outshines every ordinary lamp — close to the Kural’s image.
islam._accuracy_note: Shared lamp imagery for inner guidance; the Qur’an’s lamp is divine light, not the human virtue of truthfulness.

judaism.quote_or_event: “O send out thy light and thy truth: let them lead me; let them bring me unto thy holy hill, and to thy tabernacles.”
judaism.explanation: The Psalmist asks God’s light and truth to guide him like lamps on the way.
judaism.tie_back: Truth as a guiding light — the Kural’s ‘lamp that does not lie.’
judaism._accuracy_note: Light and truth are paired as guides; they are God’s gifts rather than the person’s own truthfulness.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “When this world is ever ablaze, why this laughter, why this jubilation? Shrouded in darkness, will you not see the light?”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada urges people wrapped in the darkness of ignorance to look for the true light of the Dhamma.
buddhism.tie_back: An inner light beyond ordinary lamps, sought by the wise — the Kural’s lamp.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Shared inner-light image; the Buddhist light is wisdom/Dhamma broadly, not truthfulness specifically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “He does not grasp falsehood, and he is deceived by neither god nor man, neither in deeds nor in thoughts.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Pindar describes Apollo (Loxias), the shining god of light and prophecy, as one who never touches falsehood and cannot be deceived.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In Greek myth the god of light is also the god of truth — light and truthfulness are one, as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The light/truth link comes through Apollo’s identity (Phoebus, ‘bright’); the passage itself speaks of his truthful mind, not a lamp.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “He lit a lamp in broad daylight and said, as he went about, ‘I am looking for a man.’”
philosophy.explanation: Diogenes the Cynic carried a lamp in daylight to show that ordinary light could not find a genuine human being — later retold as searching for an honest man.
philosophy.tie_back: An ordinary lamp cannot reveal the true person; only honesty does — close to the Kural’s ‘not every lamp is a lamp.’
philosophy.source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers 6.41 (tr. R. D. Hicks)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Vivid lamp parallel; the original seeks a real ‘man,’ and the ‘honest man’ reading is a later popular gloss.

kurals.tamil:
யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை எனைத்தொன்றும்
வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற.
kurals.transliteration:
Yaam meyyaak kandavatrul illai enaiththondrum
Vaaymaiyin nalla pira.
kurals.meaning: Among all the things we have found to be truly real and good, there is nothing, in any way, better than truthfulness.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you searched the whole world and all the best books for the most precious treasure. Valluvar says he did that kind of search — and the greatest treasure he found was simply telling the truth.
kurals.university: The chapter closes with a personal verdict — one of the rare places Valluvar speaks in the first person (yaam, ‘we’). ‘Meyyaak kandavai’ means ‘things seen/found as real,’ and there is a deliberate play between mey (reality, truth) and vaaymai (truthful speech): among all that is mey, nothing surpasses vaaymai. Pappaiah reads kandavai as ‘the books I have examined,’ making this a survey of all moral literature; Kalaignar takes it as the conclusion of research into what is true. Either way, the couplet sets veracity at the summit of all virtues, bringing the chapter full circle from its opening definition.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “There is no virtue equal to Truth: there is nothing superior to Truth. O king, Truth is God himself; Truth is the highest vow.”
hinduism.explanation: Shakuntala tells King Dushmanta that nothing is higher than truth — it is God himself.
hinduism.tie_back: The same verdict as the Kural: nothing in existence is better than truth.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Adi Parva, Section 74 (tr. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near-identical claim of truth’s supremacy; the Mahabharata goes further in identifying Truth with God.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Jesus saith unto him, I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus identifies himself with truth itself, the one path to God.
christianity.tie_back: Truth placed at the very summit of reality, as in the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Truth is supreme, but here it is a divine person, not the human virtue of truthful speech.

islam.quote_or_event: “Allāh will say, ‘This is the Day when the truthful will benefit from their truthfulness.’ For them are gardens [in Paradise] beneath which rivers flow… That is the great attainment.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, truthfulness is named as the quality that brings the ‘great attainment.’
islam.tie_back: Truthfulness as the final, decisive good — the Kural’s verdict.
islam._accuracy_note: Truthfulness singled out as what ultimately counts; not explicitly ranked above every other good.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Rabbi Ḥanina said: The seal of the Holy One, Blessed be He, is truth [emet].”
judaism.explanation: The Talmud says God’s own signature — the mark he sets on all things — is truth (emet, spelled with the first, middle and last letters of the Hebrew alphabet).
judaism.tie_back: If God’s own seal is truth, nothing can be higher — the Kural’s conclusion.
judaism.source: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 55a (William Davidson / Koren-Steinsaltz tr.)
judaism._accuracy_note: Truth at the highest level of reality; a theological rather than purely ethical claim.

buddhism.explanation: Asked by the demon Alavaka what is the highest of all tastes, the Buddha answers ‘truth,’ and adds: go and ask others if anything better than truth, self-control, endurance and relinquishment can be found.
buddhism.tie_back: After surveying all good things, truth stands at the top — the Kural’s verdict.
buddhism.source: Alavaka Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.10 (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Very close in spirit; the Buddha names truth first among four supreme qualities rather than alone.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “I have escaped. There is strength in my truth.”
greek_mythology.explanation: The blind prophet Teiresias, threatened by King Oedipus, answers that the truth he holds is his whole protection — and the truth indeed prevails over the king.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Truth as the strongest possession, stronger even than a king’s power.
greek_mythology.source: Sophocles, Oedipus Tyrannus 356 (tr. R. C. Jebb, rev. Alex Sens)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Truth’s supreme strength is dramatised; Teiresias speaks of prophetic truth, not truthfulness as a virtue.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Truth is the beginning of every good thing, both to Gods and men.”
philosophy.explanation: In the Laws, Plato’s Athenian says truth leads all goods, and that anyone who would be blessed should share in truth from the start of life.
philosophy.tie_back: Truth at the head of all goods — Valluvar’s closing verdict.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near-exact: truth ranked first among all goods for gods and humans.
